paragraphs.text: Dear sisters and elders, we are living in very troubled times. Just a few months ago, the mission was going strong. And then the coronavirus came and everything changed. We're confined in our houses, we could no longer get out among the people—the people we were called to serve and bless, the people we love. We could no longer meet together and be inspired by the association with one another and through the spirit that always attends our mission meetings. On top of all that, our own individual problems haven't mysteriously gone away either. We still have them. Additionally, we're concerned about our families at home, some of whom we know are suffering. And so truly these are troubled times.

Jesus's disciples also experienced a dramatic change in their lives. They had all come from various walks of life before they met Jesus. Maybe for some of them, life was good and for others, life wasn't so good. But for the past three and a half years that they had been with Jesus, life had been very good. They had seen countless miracles, healings, deliverances, walking on water, calming the storm, feeding the 5,000, and even raising the dead. They had spent those years listening to the greatest teachings ever spoken.

Further, because they expected Jesus would literally overthrow the Roman government and set up his kingdom in Jerusalem, they were excited because Jesus had gained popularity among the people and they were on the inside of the movement. I'm not saying that everything was perfect for the disciples, but by and large, life was going good for them. They had no reason to expect that in the very near future all of their expectations and hopes would fall apart. They had no idea of the crisis they were about to be put through, that Jesus would be arrested, beaten, tried, and crucified.

However, Jesus knew what was about to take place and he wanted to prepare them for what was ahead. So he explained to them what was about to happen. Previously, he had made references to his death, but in a way that they simply didn't understand. Now he wanted them to really understand what he was saying, so he spoke clearly with them. This conversation that Jesus had with them prepared them better to accept the changes and the uncertainty that was about to come upon them.

None of us likes change. None of us likes uncertainty. We're always going to have a certain level of worry when we know that hard times are ahead of us. However, we can, by examining Jesus' words to his disciples, learn how to get through these kinds of times without worrying so much.

In John 14, verses 1 through 4, we read: "Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also. And whither I go ye know, and the way ye know."

Knowing the future which lay before his disciples, Jesus gave them true doctrine to help them get through the troubled times. And the first thing he says to them is, "ye believe in God, believe also in me." This really is the foundational formula for finding peace in troubled times. Believe in Christ. All of the other things that he says to them were hinged upon that one key doctrine. Believe in him. He goes on to explain some of the reasons and ways that they can believe in him. But he never really moves beyond belief or deep faith as the thing that will get them through the troubled times.

In Philippians chapter 4, verses 6 and 7, the Apostle Paul writes: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." These verses tell us not to worry about anything, but just to pray and believe. Why? Because God is in control. What happens, happens for a reason.

When the soldiers came to arrest Jesus, it would have been easy to forget that God was in control. It may have looked very much like the Roman soldiers were in control, or the Jewish leaders were in control. And it may have even seemed that Satan was successfully overcoming the plan of God. Don't forget, the disciples' idea of the Messiah was that he would create a political kingdom in Jerusalem, overthrowing the Roman government. The death of the Messiah didn't fit into their idea at that time.

But Jesus explained to them that it was all a part of God's plan. Satan may have thought it was his idea to crucify Jesus, but he was really just playing right into God's hands. Jesus explained that he had to leave them, but it was for good reason. It was only if he left that he could prepare heaven for them. In fact, it was only by his death and resurrection that they could even get to heaven in the first place. Another reason that he is going, as he explained later on, was so that he could send the Holy Spirit.

Many times in our lives, the situations may seem hopeless. We may even question, "Where is God in all this?" We may wonder how anything good could possibly come of our situation. But then we remember this verse in Romans 8, verse 28: "And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose." No matter what the adversary throws your way, God can turn it into good if we believe in him. Remember what Jesus told Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, whose daughter had already died? "Fear not: believe only." You too can trust God. And as you do, he can do miracles for you. He didn't send trials your way, but he didn't stop them either because he plans to do something great with you through them. We may not always see right now what good is going to come of a particular difficult season or challenge, but that's where faith in God comes in. God says it will turn into good. You may see it someday, and you may never recognize it, but good will come.

The second way that Jesus reassured his disciples was his promise that it wouldn't last forever. He said, "I'm going away, but I'll be back to get you." The fact is that God promises that whatever trials you have to go through, they won't last forever. There is a saying, "all good things must come to an end." But as missionaries for the Lord's true church, our perspective should be all bad things must come to an end because we know they do. Jesus knew that his disciples couldn't survive the turmoil that was ahead forever, but he was able to promise them that there may be storm clouds ahead, but there will be sunshine on the other side. And in Psalm 30, verse 5, we read: "weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." And you may feel tonight or another night like your circumstances will never change, will never get better. You may feel like you have entered the never-ending valley of the shadow of death, but Jesus promises you that your trials will not last forever.

Another thing to remember is that everyone has troubles. Everyone has their troubled times. None of us escapes these experiences. But as we learn in 1 Corinthians chapter 10, verse 13: "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it." I believe, elders and sisters, this doesn't just mean temptation as in temptation to sin. I believe that this pertains to every kind of trial the adversary can throw our way.

You may not yet see the light at the end of a particularly troubling time. You may not see any hope, but you can trust God's word when he says that he will show you a way out. Even on the earth now he will provide a way out for you. But our ultimate release is going to come when we finish this mortal probation and enter into his rest. This particularly beloved verse from the Book of Mormon helps me keep my perspective in troubled times, in Mosiah chapter 2, verse 41: "And moreover, I would desire that ye should consider on the blessed and happy state of those that keep the commandments of God. For behold, they are blessed in all things, both temporal and spiritual; and if they hold out faithful to the end, they are received into heaven, that thereby they may dwell with God in a state of never-ending happiness. O remember, remember that these things are true; for the Lord God hath spoken it."

Job was put through a terrible trial. First, having been rich, he lost all his possessions. He lost his cattle, his house, and his children. Then Satan cursed him with a terrible sickness. Even his wife advised him to curse God and die. But in that moment, we see the most intense trust and belief in God and his deliverance when Job declared: "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God." Job knew that no matter what he was going through now, he could endure it because it wouldn't last forever. As surely as his problem existed, one day his Redeemer would stand triumphant.

I think the greatest and most powerful gift that Jesus was about to give his disciples was this: "And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you." Jesus promised them that even though he himself had to go, he would send another Comforter. He would send the Holy Spirit to them, and the Holy Spirit wouldn't be limited to time and space. Being a spirit, he could influence us at all times and in all places.

After your baptism, hands were laid upon your head, and by the power and authority of the holy priesthood, you were given the gift of the Holy Ghost. So during these troubled times, or when the going gets rough in a future day for you—maybe so rough that you're tempted to think that God has abandoned you—just remember those words spoken to you: "Receive the Holy Ghost." It is your right to receive him if you're doing your best to be worthy of him. But as the Apostle Paul says in his letter to the Hebrew members of the church: "Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee." This verse says you can be content with whatever you have, being content whatever your circumstances are, because God has promised you that he will never abandon you. He will walk right alongside you through the power of the Holy Ghost.

Then you can echo what King David said in his troubled times: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever." And it is with your faith in God and your companionship with the Holy Spirit that you will get through your tough times, no matter what you have to go through. You don't have to go alone. God will walk right beside you and see you safely through to the other side if you let him, if you invite him, if you live worthy of his blessings.

His promise of old is just as valid today as it was when he said it 2,000 years ago. It is said just as much to you as it was said to his disciples then: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid." Good night, sisters and elders. Rest well, we love you, and more importantly, God loves you.
